appendix

Why the last word is never free

A mnemonic encodes entropy plus a checksum. The word count fixes the split: every word contributes 11 bits, and the final bits of the last word are dictated by SHA-256.

wordsentropychecksumtotal bitsfree bits in last wordvalid final words
12128b4b132b7128
15160b5b165b664
18192b6b198b532
21224b7b231b416
24256b8b264b38
1 · entropy

128–256 bits from a CSPRNG. This is the only secret; everything else is derived.

2 · checksum

SHA-256(entropy) is truncated to 4 bits and appended, then the stream is cut into 11-bit indices.

3 · seed

PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(mnemonic, "mnemonic"+passphrase, 2048) yields the 512-bit BIP-32 seed.

⚠️ Security notes

  • Repeated-word patterns (abandon ×11) have almost no entropy. They are burnt into every cracking dictionary — never fund them.
  • Poetic “haiku” phrases are memorable to humans and to attackers; they are not valid mnemonics anyway, as the checksum solver shows.
  • Nothing here is transmitted or stored, but a browser is not a hardware wallet. Use real wallets for real funds.
  • Extended keys and seeds shown in this tool are exposed deliberately for education — a seed alone spends everything derived from it.
Built with @scure/bip39, @scure/bip32, @noble/hashes and @scure/base — offline, audited, dependency-light. No phrase you type ever leaves this tab. The Zen presets are original CSS Zen Garden-inspired compositions.
